The Story of Vajrakumar

I pay homage to the Jina, the supreme teacher of the world, and write here the story of Vajrakumar Muni, who practiced prabhavna — the limb of right faith that glorifies and propagates the dharma.

In Hastinapur there ruled King Bal, wise in statecraft and compassionate. His minister Garuda had a son, Somdatt, brilliant in the scriptures and handsome beyond measure.

Somdatt's Renunciation

One day Somdatt visited his uncle Subhuti in Ahichhatrapur and asked to be introduced to the king. Subhuti, swelling with pride, refused. Stung by the insult, Somdatt went directly to the king, displayed his learning, and was appointed minister himself. His uncle, seeing the young man's brilliance, gave him his daughter Yagndatta in marriage.

In time, Yagndatta conceived. During her pregnancy she craved mangoes fiercely, though it was out of season. Somdatt ventured into the forest and by fortune found a single mango tree bearing fruit. Beneath it sat a great yogi in meditation, and the tree seemed to be the very embodiment of dharma, its fruit a blessing of the sage's presence.

Somdatt plucked mangoes and sent them to his wife, then sat at the monk's feet and asked, "Master, what is the essence of life in this world?" The sage replied that dharma alone is the essence — dharma of two kinds: the monk's path of complete renunciation, and the householder's path of partial observance. Both lead towards liberation, but the monk's path reaches it in this very life.

Hearing this, Somdatt was filled with such powerful detachment that he renounced everything on the spot. He took monastic vows from the yogi, studied the scriptures deeply, and in time became a revered monk himself.

The Abandoned Child

Yagndatta, learning that her husband had become a monk, was consumed with fury. "What use is this life?" she cried. In her rage she took their infant son and left him on a remote mountain near the sage's meditation cave. What will not a woman do when blinded by anger?

But fortune favours the meritorious. A vidyadhar prince named Divakar, travelling on pilgrimage, happened to pass that way. He saw the luminous child playing near the cave and lifted him into his arms. Noticing a vajra — a thunderbolt — marked on the baby's hands, his wife named the boy Vajrakumar. They raised him as their own with great love.

Vajrakumar's Rise

Vajrakumar grew swiftly in wisdom and beauty. Studying at the court of his maternal uncle Vimalvahan, king of Kankpuri, he became a renowned scholar even in youth. One day on a mountain he encountered a young woman named Pavanvega, whose meditation he aided by removing a thorn from her eye. Grateful, she pledged herself to him, and they were duly married.

When Vajrakumar learned that his father Divakar had been driven from his kingdom by a younger brother named Purandar, he marched on Amravati with an army and his wife's supernatural powers. He defeated Purandar swiftly and restored his father to the throne. The saying proved true: "A worthy son is the lamp of the family."

But Divakar's second wife grew jealous of Vajrakumar. One day he overheard her speaking ill of him, and his heart burned. He confronted his father: "Tell me truly — whose son am I?" Divakar revealed the whole story: the mango tree, the yogi, the abandonment on the mountain. Vajrakumar was struck with profound detachment. The web of worldly life seemed terrible to him. He flew at once to pay homage to his biological father — now the monk Somdatt — and begged for initiation.

Divakar pleaded with him to stay, but Vajrakumar cast off his ornaments and took the vows of a Jain monk. He devoted himself to the harshest austerities and bore every hardship with patience, becoming a shining moon to the ocean of the Jina's teaching.

The Contest of Processions

In the city of Mathura, Queen Urvila — a devout Jain — held a grand chariot festival every year in honour of the Jina. But a second queen named Buddhdasi, who followed another faith, persuaded the king to let her chariot go first, blocking Urvila's procession.

Urvila took a vow: "My chariot shall lead, or I shall not eat." She came to Vajrakumar Muni and Somdatt Muni for help, telling them the Jain dharma was in danger. Vajrakumar summoned the vidyadhar warriors who had come to pay homage. "You are powerful, and the dharma faces a threat. Go and ensure that Queen Urvila's chariot goes first, as it has always done."

The vidyahars flew to Mathura, reasoned with Buddhdasi's guards, and when persuasion failed, scattered them in battle. Urvila's chariot rolled out in full splendour, and the Jain faith was glorified before all the people. Many abandoned false beliefs and embraced right faith. Even the king and Buddhdasi were moved by the power of the dharma and accepted the Jain path with pure hearts.

The Teaching

This is the essence of prabhavna: using one's influence, wealth, and power to honour and spread the dharma. Through consecration ceremonies, temple restoration, chariot festivals, gifts of learning, food, and fearlessness — the faithful glorify the teaching and inspire others to walk the path. Those who practice prabhavna are honoured in all three worlds and attain liberation at the end. May Vajrakumar Muni keep my mind ever firm in the Jain dharma.
